Type-2
What would be a Type-2 Error in the context of this problem?
Fail to reject the null hypothesis that \(\mu_b = \mu_{bk}\) when \(\mu_b = \mu_{bk}\) is actually false (we should have rejected)!
In order to calculate this probability (and power), we need to make an assumption on what \(\mu_b - \mu_{bk}\) actually is!
Let’s assume that \(\mu_b - \mu_{bk} = 5\).

title: Error and Power
text:
Why 5?
The true difference of 5 minutes is an assumed effect size for the purpose of calculating the probability of a Type II error. It is not something we know from the sample data.
Effect size is a quantitative measure of the magnitude of a difference, relationship, or effect in a population.
We might choose 5 because…

Previous research: Earlier studies may suggest that one type of pen lasts approximately 5 minutes longer than the other.
Practical significance: The company might consider a 5-minute difference large enough to matter when deciding which pen to manufacture or sell.

In practice, we may calculate the probability of a Type-2 error for many many different effect sizes!

Degrees of freedom
The Wardrobe Analogy
Imagine you have 7 different shirts to wear over a 7-day week. On Monday, you have 7 choices. On Tuesday, 6 choices. By the time Sunday rolls around, you only have 1 shirt left. You have no choice on Sunday—your decision was perfectly determined by the previous 6 days. You had 6 days of true flexibility, meaning your degrees of freedom are 6.

Degrees of freedom

title: Chi-Square
text:
Chi-square
The CLT isn’t what makes a chi-square statistic approximately chi-square. The expected-count conditions are related to that approximation. The CLT explains why the chi-square distribution itself becomes approximately normal as its degrees of freedom increase.
(Difference in means case): Because \(\bar X\) is a function of random variables, \(\bar X\) is itself a random variable. It’s the same thing with Chi-square!
The Central Limit Theorem tells us that sums of many independent random variables tend to become approximately normal, provided they have finite mean and variance.
\(\chi^2 = Z_1^2 + \cdots + Z_k^2\) approaches normal as degrees of freedom increase!

title: Chi-Square
text:
Things we learned
– The shape of the chi-square distribution curve depends on the degrees of freedom
– Test statistic can not be negative
– The chi-square distribution curve is skewed to the right, and the chi-square test is always right-tailed
– A chi-square test cannot have a directional hypothesis. A chi-square value can only indicate that a relationship exists between two variables, not what the relationship is.

title: Inference for two proportions (8.2)
text:
Variability
Statistics all comes down to quantifying variability/uncertainity…
We are in the hypothesis testing game of trying to figure out “did we see something unusual enough” to the point where we have evidence to reject our initial claim. We would never expect our sample statistic to be exactly our parameter value in the first place. The question isn’t are they equal, the question is is our result unusual.

title: Inference for two means (7.2)

Sampling Distribution
A linear combination of independent normal random variables is also normally distributed.
\[
\bar{X}_W \sim N\left(\mu_W,\frac{\sigma_W^2}{n_W}\right)
\]
and
\[
\bar{X}_M \sim N\left(\mu_M,\frac{\sigma_M^2}{n_M}\right)
\]
Since both variables are normal, their linear combination is normal:
\[
\bar{X}_W-\bar{X}_M
\sim
N\left(
\mu_W-\mu_M,
\frac{\sigma_W^2}{n_W}+\frac{\sigma_M^2}{n_M}
\right)
\]

text:
Difference in proportions
Conceptually, it’s very similar for a difference in proportions!
… proportions are based on binomial/random-count data, so we use the Central Limit Theorem/normal approximation rather than saying the original observations are normally distributed.
\[
\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2
\approx
N\left(
p_1 - p_2,\,
\frac{p(1-p)}{n_1}
+
\frac{p(1-p)}{n_2}
\right)
\]
